title: Saying sorry and making up
keyIdea: When you hurt or upset someone, even by accident, say sorry and say what you did: "Sorry, Mia. I knocked your tower down." Then do something to put it right: build the tower again, give the toy back, or get help for a bump. When someone says sorry to you, you can say "That is OK" and play again.

kid: Oops! Ben's ball hits Mia's tower. It falls down. Mia cries. Ben did not mean to do it. But Mia is still sad.
Ben says, "Sorry, Mia. I knocked your tower down." He says what he did. That shows he means it. Mia is still a bit sad. So Ben helps. They build the tower again, block by block. Now Mia smiles.
Each oops has its own fix. Took a toy? Give it back. Bumped a friend? Get a grown-up or a plaster. Said a mean word? Say a kind one.
When a friend says sorry to you, you can say, "That is OK." Then you can play again.
adult: This topic sits in Personal, Social and Emotional Development in the EYFS (Development Matters 2023 and the Early Learning Goals 'Building Relationships' and 'Managing Self'). It also links to the 'Respectful relationships' and 'Caring friendships' strands of DfE Relationships Education (2019) at Key Stage 1. At 4 to 5 years, children say sorry when a grown-up prompts them. The goal is that they also try to make amends: do something that repairs the harm.

A full apology for this age has three parts. First, name what you did: 'I knocked your tower down.' Second, say sorry. Third, offer a repair that fits the harm. Rebuild what was broken, return what was taken, fetch help for a hurt, or swap a hurtful word for a kind one. Many settings use this restorative approach in place of a bare 'say sorry'. The child who was hurt can then accept the apology, which is the start of forgiveness and playing together again.

Common mistakes: thinking an accident needs no sorry (a hurt is still a hurt, whatever the intent); a quick 'sorry' shouted while running off; saying sorry but keeping the toy; and thinking a sorry must be repeated over and over before you can make up. Be careful not to force a child to say a sorry they cannot yet feel. Calm first, then help them notice the other child's face, then model the words.

In the lab your child picks the sorry that names what was done. They drag the right fix-it to a sad friend: blocks, the teddy or a plaster. Then they find every child in a playground who got hurt, mend hurt words and a spill, and choose how to accept a sorry and play again.

familyTip: Next time there is a toy-room oops, try the three steps together: "What happened? Say sorry and say what you did. How can we fix it?" Praise the fix, not just the word sorry.

visual.caption: Does it help make up? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pick a good sorry, drag the right fix-it to a sad friend, say sorry to everyone who got hurt, and make up.

practice.prompt: You knocked down Mia's tower. Which is the best sorry?
choices: Sorry, Mia. I knocked your tower down.
It fell by itself!
Ha ha, it fell!
practice.hint: A good sorry says what you did. Which one does that?
practice.explain: Saying what you did shows Mia that you know what went wrong, and that you mean your sorry.

practice.prompt: You knocked over a tower of {n} blocks. You help build it again. You put back {k} blocks. How many blocks are still on the floor?
practice.hint: Start with {n} blocks on the floor. Take away the {k} you put back.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}, so {=n-k} blocks are still on the floor. Keep helping until the tower is back up.

practice.prompt: You bumped Zoe by mistake. Her knee hurts. What do you do?
choices: Say sorry and get a grown-up
Nothing. It was a mistake.
Say: You are fine, get up
practice.hint: Zoe is still hurt, even if you did not mean it.
practice.explain: A mistake can still hurt. Say sorry, then help: get a grown-up or a plaster for her knee.

practice.prompt: You took {n} of Leo's cars. You give {k} back. How many more cars do you need to give back?
practice.hint: Leo needs all {n} cars back. You gave {k}. How many are left to give?
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}. Give back {=n-k} more cars so Leo has all of his cars again.

pool.prompt: You took Kai's crayon. What fixes it?
choices: Say sorry and give it back
Say sorry and keep it
Hide it
pool.hint: Sorry is the start. What does Kai need back?
pool.explain: Saying sorry is good, but Kai needs his crayon. Giving it back puts it right.

pool.prompt: You spilled Raj's juice. What helps most?
choices: Say sorry and help wipe it up
Say: The cup did it!
Walk away
pool.hint: What would make Raj feel better about the mess?
pool.explain: Saying sorry and wiping up the juice helps fix the oops. Blaming the cup is a fib.

pool.prompt: Mia said sorry and helped fix your tower. What can you say?
choices: That is OK. Let us play!
Go away for ever!
Say sorry ten more times!
pool.hint: Mia said sorry and she helped. How do you make up?
pool.explain: One real sorry is enough. Saying 'That is OK' lets you both play again.

pool.prompt: You said Jo's picture is ugly. Jo is sad. What helps?
choices: Say sorry and say something kind about it
Say it again louder
Say nothing
pool.hint: Words can hurt too. What words could help instead?
pool.explain: Mean words hurt. Say sorry, then say something kind, like 'I like the big sun.'

pool.prompt: {a} children got hurt in the game. You have said sorry to {b} of them. How many more need a sorry?
pool.hint: Everyone who got hurt needs a sorry. Take away the ones you have done.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}, so {=a-b} more children need a sorry from you.

choices: Ana, who you bumped by mistake
Kai, who is happy on the swing
Ella, who is reading a book
pool.hint: Look for the child who got hurt.
pool.explain: Ana got hurt, even though it was a mistake, so she needs a sorry. Kai and Ella are fine.

pool.prompt: Mia's tower had {n} blocks. It fell. You and Mia build {k} blocks back. How many blocks tall is the tower now?
pool.hint: Count only the blocks that are back on the tower.
pool.explain: You built {k} blocks back, so the tower is {k} blocks tall now. Mia has {=n-k} more to go.

pool.prompt: Ben shouts 'sorry!' and runs off. Mia's tower is still on the floor. Is that enough?
choices: No. Stay and help build it again.
Yes. He said the word.
Yes, if he says it fast
pool.hint: Is the tower fixed? Is Mia still sad?
pool.explain: A sorry is the start. Ben should stay and help Mia build the tower again.
